principles.name: Habit Stacking
principles.description: Linking a new habit to an already-established habit so the existing behaviour serves as a reliable cue for the new one.
principles.mechanism: Existing habits are deeply encoded neural pathways; anchoring a new behaviour to one exploits that automaticity and reduces the need for conscious intention.
principles.source: Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones. Avery/Penguin Random House.
principles.example: After I pour my morning coffee (existing habit), I will put on my running shoes and do a 10-minute walk around the block (new habit).

principles.name: Implementation Intention
principles.description: Forming a specific when–where–how plan for a desired behaviour using the format 'When situation X occurs, I will perform response Y'.
principles.mechanism: Pre-deciding the exact context bridges the intention–action gap by creating a mental link between a situational cue and the intended response, reducing deliberation at the moment of action.
principles.source: Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.
principles.example: I will go for a 20-minute jog on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 7:00 AM from my front door, wearing my pre-laid-out gear.

principles.name: Temptation Bundling
principles.description: Pairing an activity you need to do (the habit) with an activity you genuinely enjoy (a temptation) so that the pleasurable activity is only available during the habit.
principles.mechanism: Linking an obligation to an immediate reward raises the hedonic value of the behaviour, counteracting present-bias and increasing the likelihood of initiation.
principles.source: Milkman, K. L., Minson, J. A., & Volpp, K. G. M. (2014). Holding the hunger games hostage at the gym: An evaluation of temptation bundling. Management Science, 60(2), 283–299.
principles.example: Only listen to your favourite podcast or audiobook while on the treadmill or during a strength-training session.

principles.name: Two-Minute Rule
principles.description: Scaling a habit down to a version that takes two minutes or less so that starting feels almost effortless.
principles.mechanism: Lowering the initiation threshold overcomes the activation energy barrier; once begun, momentum frequently carries the behaviour beyond the two-minute version.
principles.source: Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones. Avery/Penguin Random House.
principles.example: Commit only to putting on workout clothes and doing one press-up; the reduced barrier typically leads to completing a full workout.

principles.name: Identity-Based Habits
principles.description: Framing a habit not as an action to perform but as an expression of who you are, casting every repetition as a vote for your desired identity.
principles.mechanism: Behaviour that aligns with self-concept is intrinsically motivating and self-sustaining because people are driven to act consistently with how they see themselves.
principles.source: Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones. Avery/Penguin Random House.
principles.example: Instead of saying 'I am trying to run', say 'I am a runner' — then each completed run reinforces that identity and makes the next run more likely.

principles.name: Variable Reward
principles.description: Introducing an element of unpredictable positive reinforcement into a habit loop to sustain engagement over time.
principles.mechanism: Variable reinforcement schedules produce the highest and most persistent response rates because unpredictability triggers dopaminergic anticipation, making the behaviour intrinsically compelling.
principles.source: Fogg, B. J. (2020). Tiny Habits: The Small Changes That Change Everything. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. (Based on Skinner, B. F. operant conditioning research, 1938–1969.)
principles.example: Use a fitness app that randomly awards bonus XP or unlocks a new challenge badge upon workout completion to keep engagement high over weeks.

principles.name: Social Commitment
principles.description: Making a public or interpersonal commitment to a fitness goal so that social accountability becomes an additional motivator for follow-through.
principles.mechanism: Self-presentation concerns and social norms create external accountability; observers serve as social reinforcers and the prospect of public failure acts as a powerful aversive stimulus that motivates action.
principles.source: Bandura, A. (1977). Social Learning Theory. Prentice Hall.
principles.example: Arrange to meet a friend at the gym three mornings per week — the social obligation makes skipping sessions significantly harder.
